The Rust-and-yellow tanager (Thlypopsis ruficeps) is a small Neotropical passerine for which early life history parameters have been estimated from closely related congeners. Hatchlings emerge after an incubation period corresponding to an age at birth of 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration determined under controlled incubation at 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. The initial wet weight of these altricial nestlings is approximately 2.1 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.1 grams] at emergence, a value comparable to that recorded for the similar-sized Tangara vassorii. This modest neonatal mass places the offspring well within the typical range for thraupids of equivalent adult stature, where hatchlings are entirely dependent on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrient intake prior to the onset of feather development.

Respirometry trials conducted under standard conditions have provided insights into the energetic demands of this tanager. The basal metabolic rate, measured as the resting oxygen consumption of post-absorptive individuals, reaches 41.82 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 41.82 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when assessed at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which lies within the thermoneutral zone for the species. This metabolic datum reflects the high resting energetic costs that a bird of this body size must meet daily to sustain vital functions, particularly during periods of reproductive activity or during the energetically demanding nestling provisioning phase that follows hatching.

Reproductive output in the Rust-and-yellow tanager follows a pattern typical of many small tropical passerines. Females lay a clutch of 2 eggs [N_R_i = 2 eggs] per nesting attempt, and field observations indicate they typically complete just 1 clutch each year [F_R_i = just 1 clutch each year], a low annual frequency that may be linked to the extended period of post-fledging care. Under the same thermal conditions that characterize active adult metabolism at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the annual reproductive output is thus defined by this combination. This conservative strategy stands in contrast to the multiple broods observed in some temperate-dwelling thraupids, suggesting an adaptive response to seasonally stable but resource-limited tropical environments.

A sequence of developmental milestones marks the transition from dependent nestling to independent juvenile in this species, all framed within the thermal environment of the active metabolic period at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Fledging, the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and leaves the nest, occurs 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty, defined as the attainment of sexual maturity and the onset of gonadal development, follows considerably later at 45 days after hatching [tp = 45 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the time required for the juvenile to complete skeletal growth and accumulate sufficient body condition at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The first successful breeding event, or time since birth at first brood, is not initiated until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a full year later at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Longevity records for the Rust-and-yellow tanager, derived from wild banding studies and supplemented by observations of captive individuals, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.3 years [am = approximately 7.3 years] under typical conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This lifespan is consistent with the slow pace of life characteristic of many small-bodied tropical rainforest birds, which tend to exhibit extended survival in exchange for reduced annual reproductive effort. The asymptotic body mass ultimately attained by adult females is 11.3 grams [Wwi = 11.3 grams], a value that represents the maximum recorded wet weight for reproductively mature individuals. This combination of a modest neonatal mass of approximately 2.1 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.1 grams] and a sevenfold increase to adult size underscores the substantial growth trajectory that the nestling must complete during its brief period of parental dependence, before achieving the nutritional independence that characterizes the free-living juvenile stage.
